    #69245. 101 fun questions for your kids to laugh, talk, and connect

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2736 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

    101 fun questions for your kids to laugh, talk, and connect

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Have you ever asked your child what they did at school only to be told, “I don’t remember…”?
    • Many kids have a magical ability to give the least amount of detail possible when asked a direct question.
    • The thing is, kids actually do want to talk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have you ever asked your child what they did at school only to be told, “I don’t remember…”?

    Many kids have a magical ability to give the least amount of detail possible when asked a direct question. It’s almost like they’re professionally trained in the art of dodging conversation.

    The thing is, kids actually do want to talk. You just have to ask the right questions: ones that spark their imagination, make them laugh, or invite them to share something meaningful on their terms.

    In a recent development, so, meet them where they are. Instead of the same old, “How was your day?” (which, let’s be honest, will never yield a thrilling response), try questions that make them pause and think for a moment. This way, you’re not prying information out of them, you’re building a habit of open conversation, one fun question at a time.

    Ask them in the car, at bedtime, over breakfast, or whenever your kid is in a chatty mood. You might be surprised at what they share — and the hilarious, heartwarming, or even unexpectedly deep conversations that follow.

    Laughter is one of the easiest ways to connect with your child (and can boost your mental health too). These offbeat, ridiculous questions will get them giggling while giving you a glimpse into their wonderfully weird little minds.

    Sources indicate that would you rather have a banana for a nose or popcorn for ears? Kids love absurd choices, and these “would you rather” questions are a surefire way to spark hilarious debates.

    Would you rather have spaghetti for hair or marshmallows for fingers?

    Would you rather live in a house made of chocolate or a castle made of cheese?

    Would you rather always talk in rhymes or only be able to whisper?

    Would you rather ride a roller coaster that never ends or a Ferris wheel that goes super fast?

    Would you rather have a pet dragon or a pet unicorn?

    Ever wonder what your backpack thinks about your daily routine? These questions help kids think outside the box — and maybe appreciate their favorite objects a little more.

    If your socks could talk, what would they say about your feet?

    If your toothbrush had feelings, how would it feel about its job?

    If your toys threw a party while you were sleeping, what would they do?

    If your backpack could complain, what would it say?

    If animals could talk to you, which one do you think would be the funniest?

    What if the moon really was made of cheese? These questions let kids build wild, imaginary worlds where anything is possible.

    If you could invent a new holiday, what would it be called and how would we celebrate?

    If your shadow had a mind of its own, what do you think it would do?

    If you could make one silly law that everyone had to follow, what would it be?

    What do you wish clouds were made of?

    If you had a magic remote that could pause or rewind real life, when would you use it?

    Sources indicate that what’s better than food? Food-related nonsense! These questions are perfect for mealtime giggles.

    What’s the silliest pizza topping combination you can think of?

    If you could turn any food into a superhero, which one would you pick and why?

    If vegetables could talk, which one would be the grumpiest?

    If you ate only dessert for an entire day, which treats would you choose?

    If you could invent a new ice cream flavor, what would it be?

    💙 Why not incorporate some silly moves into your kids day with Mel Mah’s Working Out the Wiggles session?

    Forget the usual “What’s your favorite color?” These questions dig a little deeper into what makes your child them — their dreams, their interests, and how they see the world.

    Who are they, really? These questions help kids define what makes them special. Who knows? They might even surprise themselves with their answers.

    What’s something you love doing that makes you feel really happy?

    If you could rename yourself, what would you want to be called?

    What’s something you’re really good at?

    What’s one thing that makes you feel really proud of yourself?

    If you had to describe yourself in three words, what would they be?

    Every kid has dreams. These questions encourage them to think massive.

    If you could have any job in the world when you grow up, what would it be?

    If you could live anywhere in the world, where would it be?

    If you could suddenly have super-skill, what would it be?

    If you could invent something to make life easier, what would it do?

    What’s something you dream about doing one day?

    In a recent development, what’s school really like? What do they wish adults understood? These questions help you see the world through their eyes.

    If you could be principal of your school for a day, what rules would you change?

    What’s one thing about school that you really like?

    What’s one thing about school you wish was different?

    What’s the best thing about being a kid?

    What’s one thing you wish adults understood about being a kid?

    Forget the usual “favorite color” and “favorite food” questions — these favorites are a little more unexpected.

    If you could only listen to one song forever, what would it be?

    If you could only watch one movie over and over again, which one would you pick?

    If you could only eat three foods for a year, what would they be?

    What book should everyone read at least once?

    If you were a baseball player, what song would play when you came up to bat?

    These questions help kids think outside the box and explore upcoming ideas — without it feeling like homework.

    What if everything was upside down? What if people lived in the ocean? These questions let kids stretch their creativity and invent a world of their own.

    If you could switch lives with any fictional character, who would it be?

    If you could time travel, would you rather visit the past or the future?

    If you could build a brand-latest planet, what would it be like?

    If you could talk to any historical figure, who would you pick and what would you ask?

    If you could live in any book or movie world, which one would you choose?

    Kids love hypotheticals, especially ridiculous ones. These questions tap into their curiosity and creativity.

    If aliens landed in our backyard, what would be the first thing you’d say to them?

    If you could talk to animals, what’s the first thing you’d ask them?

    If you could change one thing about the world, what would it be?

    If you could be invisible for a day, what would you do?

    If you could wake up with a superpower, which one would you want?

    Kids are natural philosophers. Sometimes, they just need the right question to get them going.

    What’s something you’ve always been curious about but never asked?

    If you could solve one significant mystery in the world, what would it be?

    If you could design your dream school, what classes would you add?

    What’s something that happens in nature that seems magical to you?

    What do you think is the coolest invention ever made?

    These questions encourage kids to see things in a upcoming way, whether it’s about themselves, the world, or the future.

    What’s something small that can make a big difference?

    What’s a time when you changed your mind about something?

    If you could ask the president one question, what would it be?

    What’s one way kids can change the world?

    What’s something you wish you knew how to do?

    Sources indicate that kids may not always have the words to explain their feelings, but these thoughtful questions help create a safe space for them to share what’s in their hearts. The Feelings Wheel can be a good visual aid for this too.

    Sometimes, kids just need the right words to talk about how they feel. These questions give them a way to open up.

    What’s something that made you feel really happy this week?

    What’s a time when you felt really proud of yourself?

    What’s something that always makes you feel loved?

    What’s a time when you felt really brave?

    What’s something you wish people knew about you?

    It’s not always easy to talk about the hard stuff, but these questions can help kids express their feelings in a safe way.

    What’s something that helps you feel better when you’re sad?

    What’s a time when something felt really hard, but you got through it?

    What’s one thing that makes you feel nervous?

    What’s something you do when you’re feeling frustrated?

    What’s a time when someone helped you feel better?

    Friends are a huge part of kids’ lives — these questions help them reflect on what friendship means to them.

    What do you think makes someone a good friend?

    What’s one way you like to show kindness to others?

    What do your friends do to make you feel special?

    What’s something you love doing with your family?

    If you could proposal the perfect day with your best friend, what would you do?

    Slowing down and noticing the good things is a skill kids can carry with them for life. These questions make space for reflection.

    What’s something you’re really grateful for today?

    What’s a small thing that makes a substantial difference in your day?

    What’s a memory that always makes you smile?

    What’s something you love about yourself?

    What’s one thing you want to remember about being a kid when you’re older?

    These questions are designed to spark deeper connections and create shared experiences — because the best conversations are about connecting.

    Every family has inside jokes, traditions, and funny moments. These questions bring them to the surface.

    What’s your favorite family tradition?

    If you could blueprint a dream family vacation, where would we go?

    What’s something funny that has happened in our family?

    What’s a meal we should cook together soon?

    If we could create a secret family handshake, what would it look like?

    Remember that time we all got soaked in the rain? Or the time you laughed so hard you snorted? These questions help relive the best moments.

    What’s the best day you’ve ever had?

    What’s something we’ve done together that made you laugh really hard?

    What’s the silliest story I’ve ever told you?

    What’s one thing we should do more often as a family?

    In a recent development, what’s next for our family? These questions invite kids to dream up exciting adventures — real or imagined.

    If we could go on a wild adventure tomorrow, what would we do?

    What’s a hobby or activity you’d love for us to try together?

    If you could design the perfect family game night, what would we play?

    If we could time travel together, what era would we visit?

    If we started a family business, what would we sell?

    Every family has its own kind of magic. These questions bring it out in unexpected ways.

    If our family had a theme song, what would it be?

    If we could invent a new family tradition, what would it be?

    If you could give everyone in our family a superpower, what would they be?

    If every member of our family was an animal, what would it be?

    What’s a way we can make someone else’s day better together?

    What’s one thing you want me to always remember about you?

    💙 Mel Mah’s Kids Bedtime Routine can help you all wind down in a peaceful way, together.

    In a recent development, the best questions to ask kids are open-ended, playful, and relevant to their world. Instead of asking, “Did you have a good day?”—which almost always leads to a dead-end answer—try something that sparks their imagination or invites storytelling, like “What was the funniest thing that happened today?” or “If you could switch places with your teacher for a day, what would you do?” Kids are much more likely to engage when a question feels fun, unexpected, and free of pressure.

    Sources indicate that kids love absurdity, so the weirder and wackier the question, the better. Offbeat questions tap into their creativity, making conversation feel more like a game than a chore.

    Silly questions are also a great way to bond, especially when you play along. If your kid tells you they’d rather ride a roller coaster that never stops over a Ferris wheel that goes super fast, ask why and join in the fun by sharing your own ridiculous answer.

    Laughter is a powerful connector, and sometimes the most unexpected conversations start with a totally goofy question.

    According to recent reports, for 6-year-olds, short questions about things they can picture work best. Silly choices and pretend play go over well. Try “What would you name a pet cloud?” or “If your stuffed animals had jobs, what would they be?” Many of the funny questions above fit this age, especially the “would you rather” and “If your stuff could talk” lists. Ask one question at a time, since young kids can lose the thread when you ask two at once.

    Which question to ask depends on what you want from the chat. If you want laughs, pick a “would you rather” or other funny question. If you want to know your child better, choose from the get-to-know list. For major feelings, try the emotional expression questions. When you’re not sure, start silly to help them relax, then move to a deeper one.

    Kids spend a lot of their day being told what to do—sit still, follow directions, finish their homework—so having a space where they get to lead the conversation is powerful. Asking fun and engaging questions gives them a chance to express themselves, think creatively, and feel heard without any right or wrong answers. It also helps build communication skills, emotional intelligence, and a sense of connection with you.

    Beyond that, these questions create opportunities for everyday bonding. A quick chat in the car or during dinner can turn into a meaningful moment of connection. The more kids feel like their thoughts and ideas are valued, the more likely they are to open up — not just about the silly stuff but about the significant things, too.

    The key to getting good answers is making the conversation feel natural, not forced. If you ask a question and get a one-word response, don’t panic — sometimes kids just need a little extra space to warm up. Try following up with, “Tell me more!” or sharing your own answer first to get the ball rolling. If they see that you’re genuinely interested (and willing to be a little silly yourself), they’ll be more likely to engage.

    According to recent reports, also, be thoughtful about your timing. Some kids open up more when they’re relaxed—like at bedtime or when you’re doing an activity together—while others chat more when they’re distracted, like in the car. If they’re tired, hungry, or mid-screen time, you might not get much out of them. But if you catch them in the right moment, you might just unlock a goldmine of thoughts, ideas, and hilarious kid logic.

    The best time to ask kids questions is when they’re naturally more open to conversation — when they feel safe, relaxed, and not pressured to respond. For some kids, that’s during bedtime, when they’re winding down and their thoughts start to flow. For others, it’s in the car, when there’s no pressure for eye contact and they can talk freely. Meal times, walks, or even while playing with Legos can also be great moments to slip in a fun question.

    Recent findings suggest that trying to force deep conversation right after school when their brain is fried or when they’re engrossed in a game or show usually won’t work. Instead, look for organic, low-pressure moments when chatting feels easy. And remember, it’s not about when you ask, it’s about showing up consistently so that when they are ready to talk, they know you’ll be there to listen.

    The Clearest Sign Of The Winter Blues

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (404 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry?
    • Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry?
    • Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

    Energy, mood or sleep lost to worry? A UK survey found a clearer winter pattern for one of the three.

    Low energy is the clearest sign of the winter blues among three symptoms studied in young people in the UK, ahead of low mood and losing sleep over worry.

    Low mood is also more pronounced in winter, although the difference is smaller.

    Shorter days may play a part by shifting the body clock and affecting when young people feel alert, while changes in exercise and social routines could also contribute.

    The researchers analysed almost 6,000 interviews with over 4,000 people aged 16 to 24 who took part in the UK’s Understanding Society survey.

    They compared interviews conducted in December, January and February with those conducted during the rest of the year, using data from 2022 and 2023 for the main analysis.

    On a 0–100 scale, the average score for low energy was about 3 points higher in winter, while the score for low mood was about 2 points higher.

    The estimate for sleep lost through worry was smaller and compatible with no seasonal difference.

    The figures describe differences between survey reports collected at different times of year, so they give a picture of the group average rather than trace how any one person’s symptoms changed.

    Earlier Canadian survey research found that a wider range of depressive symptoms varied by season among young people than among older adults (Lukmanji et al., 2020).

    Sleep schedules continue to shift through adolescence and into early adulthood, so the timing of daylight may influence when young people feel most alert.

    Winter can also change the shape of an ordinary week, with fewer chances to be active outdoors or spend time with friends in person.

    Feeling short of energy could make it harder to stay engaged through a day of lessons or a long shift, even when the person’s mood has barely changed.

    The study was published in the journal PLOS ONE (Guan et al., 2026).

    #69243. Breaking: What’s Fogging Your Brain? Signs of Aging vs. ADHD

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (759 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Additudemag ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: What’s Fogging Your Brain? Signs of Aging vs. ADHD

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.
    • Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?
    • ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.

    Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?

    ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other. While ADHD symptoms involve forgetfulness, inattention, and distractibility, MCI has specific cognitive symptoms of word-finding challenges, misspellings, and the use of generic terms like “stuff” and “things” because of word-finding difficulty. Also, MCI is progressive over two to three years, whereas ADHD doesn’t generally worsen.

    It has been revealed that in perimenopause, a decline in estrogen leads to cognitive difficulties. In contrast to MCI, we know that the cognitive changes from estrogen decline are not the result of neurodegeneration.

    According to recent reports, however, the specific deficits related to declining estrogen haven’t been well differentiated from those associated with ADHD. So if you have pre-existing ADHD and you experience heightened cognitive difficulties in perimenopause and menopause, you may think, “My ADHD is getting worse.” But it’s likely not worsening ADHD. It’s declining estrogen.

    Industry observers note that okay, so what do you do about it? There is a paucity of research for clinical guidance. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was not always recommended because it was alleged to increase risk for breast cancer and other illnesses. That claim has now been refuted by the most recent research, which has led to the removal of the black box warning from the FDA on HRT product labels. And so, if I have a female patient with ADHD who is 50 years old and claims, “For the past two years, I’ve had cognitive decline,” the question to consider is this: “Do I increase her stimulant medication or do I put her on HRT?”.

    According to recent reports, I am inclined at that point to put her on HRT for three months, keep her stimulant medication dosage stable, and monitor the qualitative changes in her cognitive functioning. If there is improvement on HRT, then the question becomes, “Does she stay on HRT for some extended period of time along with the stimulant medication?” If the HRT doesn’t work or she can’t take HRT for medical reasons, then I might increase the stimulant medication dosage to see if we can’t overcome the perimenopausal changes from the estrogen decline. This advice comes from my clinical experience, and it is unfortunate that we don’t have more research for clinical guidance here.

    [Take This Self-Test: Is It Perimenopause or ADHD?].

    Q: Could ADHD stimulant medication mask symptoms of mild cognitive impairment?

    There is very limited research on stimulants and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). My clinical impression is that stimulants likely improve symptoms of MCI, but do not take that as an endorsement to seek treatment for MCI with stimulants. There is emerging research on MCI and stimulants that has not yet been published. The follow-up question to that is, if you have ADHD and MCI, will treating the ADHD delay the development of MCI or Alzheimer’s? There is no clinical research for me to answer that question. But if this were me, I’d be treating my ADHD, keeping my fingers crossed, and appreciating the fact that the quality of my life on medicine is better than it would be without my ADHD treated.

    Q: Does ADHD get worse as you get older?

    ADHD should not get worse; however, the experience of ADHD may be worse if life’s demands start to increase and exceed your ability to compensate. However, if you’re having cognitive changes that are beyond the scope of your ADHD, you may have two neurologic processes going on: your ADHD and something else. In this case, your ADHD may, indeed, be getting worse because you have a second neurological process that needs to be evaluated.

    In a recent development, david W. Goodman, M.D., is an internationally recognized expert on adult ADHD.

    Tech Report: Empathy vs compassion: the difference (with real-life examples)

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that understanding and connecting with another person—either through empathy or compassion—facilitates more meaningful interactions and relationships.
    • Knowing the differences between empathy and compassion can help us approach others and what they’re going through with understanding and kindness.
    • Compassion is concern for another person's well-being and happiness, and a genuine urge to help alleviate their suffering.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

    Recent findings suggest that understanding and connecting with another person—either through empathy or compassion—facilitates more meaningful interactions and relationships. Whether it’s a friend going through a tough time or a family member facing a challenge, how we connect with them can significantly impact the support we offer.

    Knowing the differences between empathy and compassion can help us approach others and what they’re going through with understanding and kindness.

    Compassion is concern for another person's well-being and happiness, and a genuine urge to help alleviate their suffering. Compassion isn’t just a fleeting emotion — it’s a lasting state, a readiness to extend a helping hand whenever possible. (For the full definition, here’s our guide to what compassion is.).

    Recent findings suggest that empathy is the capability to tune into someone else’s emotions and to feel what they’re feeling. Empathy means genuinely trying to understand another person’s feelings and perspective.

    💙 Sharpen your listening skills and make others truly feel heard with Jay Shetty in this Supportive Listening meditation.

    In a recent development, while both empathy and compassion are avenues to connect with others, their core essence and impact are different. While empathy allows for emotional understanding, compassion takes it further by driving action. It's about moving from feeling to doing, from emotional resonance to proactive kindness.

    Through this understanding, we can see the value of cultivating empathy and practicing compassion in our daily actions, which not only enrich our relationships but positively impact our communities, too.

    Empathy steers emotional connection. It's about feeling the same emotions that another person is experiencing and aligning emotionally because of that similarity. On the other hand, compassion drives us towards a deep understanding of another's distress, coupled with a desire to make them feel better. It's not just about feeling, it’s about understanding and taking action.

    Empathy is rooted in deeply feeling what another person is going through and mirroring their emotional state. Compassion is about acknowledging what the other people are going through instead of feeling the emotion yourself.

    Industry observers note that empathy often revolves around an inward reflection that allows us to feel the emotions that another person is experiencing. Compassion propels us outward and encourages acting on the feeling to help alleviate someone else’s discomfort.

    Recent findings suggest that empathy primarily consists of feeling the emotional state of another, while compassion is action-oriented. Compassion prompts us to take steps to ease another's suffering, no matter how small.

    Recent findings suggest that empathy, although a profound feeling, can be more of a momentary emotional connection that is often fleeting once the shared emotion dissipates. Compassion, on the other hand, reflects a long-term commitment to assisting others and a consistent readiness to help.

    💙 Learn more about Empathy vs. Compassion with this Daily Jay session.

    Industry observers note that you usually won’t choose between them in the moment. They tend to show up together. Here’s how each one can look in the same situation.

    In a recent development, empathy is feeling with someone. Compassion is taking a step to help. You won’t usually pick one in the moment, since feeling with someone is often what leads you to help.

    In a recent development, empathy and compassion are ways to connect with others, but they play different roles. Empathy is about feeling the same emotions that someone else is feeling. For example, if a friend is sad, you feel sad along with them. Compassion takes empathy a step further. It’s about recognizing someone’s distress and wanting to help alleviate it. So, when you see someone in trouble, not only do you understand their problem, but you also want to help sort it out. Compassion motivates us to act and make a positive difference, while empathy encourages us to feel and relate.

    Both empathy and compassion are valuable in building meaningful relationships. Empathy helps in understanding other people’s emotions and creating bonds. Compassion, however, not only understands but also propels us to take action to help. It’s about moving from feeling to doing something helpful. Empathy can be a stepping stone to compassion, leading us from feeling to taking positive action.

    In a recent development, being empathetic and compassionate is like having a superpower for creating solid and supportive relationships. Empathy allows you to understand others' feelings, while compassion motivates you to take action to help. It’s a blend that encourages understanding while making a positive impact in others’ lives. Empathy and compassion go hand in hand, enhancing our connections with others and making our social interactions more meaningful and enriching.

    In a recent development, empathetic and compassionate leadership both aim to create a supportive work environment, but they do so in slightly different ways. Empathetic leadership is about understanding employees' emotions and perspectives and creating an environment where people feel heard and understood. Compassionate leadership, on the other hand, not only understands but takes action to support and help employees, recognizing the challenges and actively working to provide support or solutions. Compassionate leadership often brings a more supportive and caring work culture, benefiting both employees and the organization.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.
    • First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.

    Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.

    First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

    Let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

    [Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

    This sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

    Finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

    It’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to blueprint. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

    Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

    For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”.

    [Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

    I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1405 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: World Kindness Day 2026: what it is and 7 ways to join in

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The barista is ringing up the person in front of you when their card gets declined.
    • Sources indicate that moments like this are what World Kindness Day is all about.
    • Read on for the story behind the day, what the research says about kindness and mental health, and some simple ways to take part, whatever your schedule looks like.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    The barista is ringing up the person in front of you when their card gets declined. You lean over, tap your phone, and cover the $4. They turn around, flustered, and thank you twice. The line keeps moving, but your morning feels a bit lighter.

    Sources indicate that moments like this are what World Kindness Day is all about. Every year on November 13, it celebrates how acts of goodwill can brighten an ordinary day, for those receiving and performing them.

    Read on for the story behind the day, what the research says about kindness and mental health, and some simple ways to take part, whatever your schedule looks like.

    World Kindness Day is an unofficial global observance that encourages acts of kindness, significant and small. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 13. The day was first observed in 1998 and grew out of the World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations rather than a single founder.

    It has been revealed that the coalition formed at a conference in Tokyo, and it included founding members from Japan, Singapore, Australia, Canada, Thailand, the U.K., and the U.S. They chose November 13 because it was the conference’s opening day and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement. Today, classrooms, offices, and communities around the world honor the day.

    Industry observers note that you’ve probably felt it: you do something kind and your mood instantly lifts. Researchers have studied this effect, and here’s what they’ve found.

    In a recent development, in a 2023 study from The Ohio State University, 122 adults with moderate to severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were assigned to one of three activities for several weeks. They either did acts of kindness, planned social activities, or practiced cognitive reappraisal, which means looking at a stressful event from a upcoming angle.

    Industry observers note that all three activities helped, but kindness did more than cognitive reappraisal to ease depression and anxiety. The kindness group was also the only one that reported feeling more connected to others.

    Other research points the same way. A review of 27 studies covering more than 4,000 people indicated that performing acts of kindness gave people a modest but noticeable boost in their well-being.

    Industry observers note that kindness may also lighten a hard day. In a two-week diary study of 77 adults, people tracked their stress, their mood, and how they helped others each day. Stress usually dragged positive emotion down, but on high-stress days when people helped more than usual, their mood held steady. In other words, a little extra kindness seemed to cushion the blow of a stressful day.

    In a recent development, A note on the research: Most of this research is short-term and relies on self-reported mood, so we can’t say how long the benefits last. Kindness can support your well-being, but it doesn’t replace professional care. If anxiety, low mood, or stress lasts for weeks, it’s worth talking to a doctor.

    Recent findings suggest that you don’t need a grand gesture. These seven ideas fit into a regular day, whether you’re at home, at work, or anywhere in between. You can also adjust any of them to fit your time, energy, and budget.

    There’s probably someone on your mind — a friend you know is having a hard time, a relative you haven’t caught up with lately, or an old coworker you miss.

    Mention the moment you thought of them, like “Saw a dog that looked like yours and had to say hi. Hope you’re doing okay.” Add “no need to reply” at the end, in case they’re feeling down or overwhelmed and might not have the energy for a back-and-forth.

    💙 Before you send your message, read our guide to loving-kindness meditation.

    Leave a short review for a small business, or send a note to a service worker who made your day. Write what you appreciated, such as the waiter who kept checking on your table or the mechanic who explained the repair without talking down to you.

    For a coworker, send a note to their manager, who may not otherwise hear about their good work.

    💙 Reflect on who you want to thank with the 7 Days of Gratitude course on Calm.

    In a recent development, A quick “love your shoes” is nice, but a more specific compliment highlights someone that you’re really paying attention, and that you care. Praise someone for how patient they were with a difficult customer or how useful their point was in the meeting.

    It takes only a few seconds, but noticing the details can mean more to someone than you might expect.

    💙 Sharpen your compliments with Jay Shetty’s Effective Praise session on Calm.

    Look for small things that would make someone’s day better and take care of one: carry the heavy bag, refill the empty printer, or take on the household chore nobody wants to do.

    When you spot a need early, you can spare someone the awkwardness of asking.

    💙 Keep the kindness moving with Jay Shetty’s Pay It Forward session on Calm.

    Sources indicate that buy lunch for your colleague, round up a tip, or add a friend’s drink to your order. Set an amount before you head out, so a kind impulse doesn’t turn into a money worry later.

    If your budget is a concern, the next idea includes free ways to help.

    Many organizations also offer remote tasks, like writing cards or tutoring online.

    💙 Start close to home with Jay Shetty’s Community Service session on Calm.

    Kindness toward yourself counts, and it’s often overlooked. Notice how you talk to yourself when something goes wrong, then ask whether you’d say it that way to a friend. If you wouldn’t, here’s a quick way to try a kinder tone.

    Try: A short self-compassion pause. Place a hand on your chest, take one slow breath, and name how you feel (“this is a lot right now”). Then say what you’d tell a friend in the same situation (“that sounds hard”).

    💙 Press play on Calm’s Friend on the Inside meditation with Jeff Warren.

    Sources indicate that the World Kindness Movement created the day to encourage kind acts around the world. For many people, it’s also an invitation to do the kind thing they’ve been putting off, like thanking a neighbor.

    Industry observers note that world Kindness Day in 2026 is on Friday, November 13. It falls on November 13 every year, so only the day of the week changes.

    World Kindness Day is on November 13 because it was the opening day of the first World Kindness Movement conference in Tokyo, and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement.

    No single person started World Kindness Day. The World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations from seven countries, launched the day in Tokyo.

    No, World Kindness Day and Random Acts of Kindness Day are two separate observances. World Kindness Day is November 13, while Random Acts of Kindness Day is February 17. They share the same spirit, so you’re welcome to celebrate both.

    Studies suggest kindness can be good for you. Acts of kindness have been linked to better mood, lower anxiety, and stronger connection with others.

    In one diary study, stressful days usually made people feel less happy and upbeat. But on days when people helped others more than usual, that drop in positive feelings was smaller.

    Recent findings suggest that kindness supports well-being, but it doesn’t replace care. Speak to a doctor if anxiety, stress, or low mood lasts for weeks.

    💙 Here’s how you can lower your stress naturally.

    If you’re feeling drained, it’s okay to start with yourself. A kind word to yourself counts, and some days it’s all you have energy for. When you have more to give, something small and thoughtful is plenty, like holding the door for someone or letting someone go ahead of you in line.

    It has been revealed that there’s no official color for World Kindness Day, so you can wear whatever feels good. Some schools and groups pick a color for their own events.
